title: Frequency Tables, Grouped Data and Pie Charts
seo_title: Sec 2 Frequency tables and grouped data Worksheets: Free Secondary 2 Maths with Answers (MOE Syllabus)
standard_text: calculation of the mean for grouped data; analysis and interpretation of tables, bar graphs, pie charts and histograms
meta_desc: Free Secondary 2 statistics worksheets: mean, median, mode and range from a frequency table, grouped data with modal class and estimated mean, pie chart angles and choosing charts. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Mean from a table = Σ(value × frequency) ÷ total frequency.
key_sub: For grouped data, use the midpoints to estimate the mean. For a pie chart, each item is 360° ÷ total.
body_html:
How it works

For a frequency table, the total frequency is how many values there are. Mean = Σ(value × frequency) ÷ total frequency. The mode is the value with the highest frequency. For the median, count through the frequencies to the middle value.

For grouped data, use the midpoint of each class to estimate the mean. The modal class has the highest frequency.

For a pie chart, each item gets 360° ÷ total frequency.

Example

Values 1, 2, 3 have frequencies 5, 3, 2. Find the mean.

Σ = 5 + 6 + 6 = 17.

17 ÷ 10.

Answer: 1.7

Example

30 people are surveyed and 8 choose walking. Find the pie chart angle.

360 ÷ 30 = 12° per person.

8 × 12.

Answer: 96°

Common mistakes

  • Adding the frequencies and dividing by the number of rows instead of finding Σ(value × frequency).
  • Giving the highest frequency as the mode instead of its value.
  • Using the end of each class instead of the midpoint to estimate the mean.
  • Dividing 360 by the number of categories instead of the total frequency.

faq.q: How do I find the mean from a frequency table?
faq.a: Multiply each value by its frequency, add these up, and divide by the total frequency.

faq.q: Why is the mean of grouped data an estimate?
faq.a: Because you use the midpoint of each class, not the exact values.
The class (group) with the highest frequency.

faq.q: How do I work out pie chart angles?
faq.a: Divide 360° by the total frequency to get the angle for one item, then multiply by each frequency.

items.q: In a pie chart, a sector of 90° represents 15 people. How many people are there altogether?
items.e: 90° is a quarter of 360°, so the total is 4 × 15 = 60.

items.q: Why is the mean from a grouped frequency table only an estimate?
c: Because the classes are different widths
Because we do not know the exact values in each class
items.e: We use the midpoint of each class instead of the real values, so it is an estimate.

items.q: The midpoint of the class 20 < x ≤ 30 is…
Two pie charts show different numbers of students: 30 in class A and 60 in class B. The “walk” sector is 120° in both. Which class has more walkers?
items.e: A: 120/360 × 30 = 10. B: 120/360 × 60 = 20. So class B (the angles are the same, but the totals are different).

items.q: A bar chart's vertical axis starts at 50 instead of 0. Why could this be misleading?
c: It makes the bars too wide
It makes small differences look large
items.e: Starting above zero makes small differences look large.

items.q: Which average can you find from a grouped frequency table exactly?
c: None of them exactly — only the modal class
items.e: Without the raw data you can only give the modal class and estimates of the others: only the modal class.

items.q: A table shows shoe sizes 4, 5, 6, 7 with frequencies 3, 8, 6, 3. What is the mode?
items.e: Size 5 has the highest frequency (8): 5.

items.q: A frequency table has values 2, 4, 6 with frequencies 1, 1, 8. Which is larger, the mean or the median?
c: The median (6) is larger than the mean (5.4)
items.e: Mean = (2 + 4 + 48) ÷ 10 = 5.4. Median = 6. So the median is larger.

items.q: What does each bar in a bar chart of frequencies show?
c: The total of all the data
How many times each value or category occurs
items.e: The height of a bar is the frequency: how many times that value or category occurs.
